name: Verb
subtitle: Verbs: present tense, commands and help verbs

ruleCards.title: Present tense: -r
ruleCards.rule: The present tense ends in -r. The form is the same for every person: jag, du, hon, vi, ni, de.
ruleCards.watch: Never change the verb for the person: jag pratar, du pratar, de pratar. Vara is irregular: jag är, du är.

fun.sv: Jag dricker kaffe, du dricker kaffe, vi dricker kaffe. Finland fungerar.
fun.en: I drink coffee, you drink coffee, we drink coffee. Finland works.
fun.note: Dricker stays the same for every person.

ruleCards.title: Verb groups I–IV
ruleCards.rule: Group I: -a becomes -ar. Group II: -a becomes -er. Group III: short verbs that don’t end in -a just add -r. Group IV: irregular verbs; most also take -er in the present.
ruleCards.watch: Group II verbs whose stem ends in r add nothing: höra → hör, köra → kör.

fun.sv: Jag pratar, du lyssnar, vi bor här. Men katten bestämmer.
fun.en: I talk, you listen, we live here. But the cat decides.
fun.note: Pratar and lyssnar are Group I, bor is Group III, bestämmer is Group II.

ruleCards.title: Which group is a new verb?
ruleCards.rule:
Ask in this order.
1. No -a at the end (bo, tro, sy)? Group III.
2. Ends in -era (studera, reparera)? Group I.
3. A new or borrowed verb (googla, mejla, chatta)? Group I.
4. Otherwise check the present tense: -ar means Group I, -er means Group II or IV.
If you have to guess, guess Group I: about two in three verbs are there.
ruleCards.watch: A few short verbs are irregular, so Group IV, not III: gå, stå, se, få, ge. Group II and IV look the same in the present; only the past shows it. A vowel change and no -de/-te (skriva → skrev) means Group IV.

fun.sv: Jag googlar vilken grupp googla är. Svaret: grupp I, som nästan alla nya verb.
fun.en: I google which group googla is. The answer: Group I, like almost all new verbs.
fun.note: Borrowed verbs go to Group I: googla, googlar, googlade, googlat.

ruleCards.title: The dictionary trick: four forms
ruleCards.rule: Dictionaries and word lists give a verb in four forms: infinitive, present, past, supine. The present tells you Group I or not. The past tells you Group II or IV.
ruleCards.watch: When you write down a new verb, write all four forms, not just the infinitive. Then you never have to guess again.

fun.sv: Ordboken säger: köpa, köper, köpte, köpt. Min plånbok säger: aj, aj, aj, aj.
fun.en: The dictionary says: buy, buys, bought, bought. My wallet says: ouch, ouch, ouch, ouch.
fun.note: Four forms, four ouches. Köpa is Group II, and p gives -te: köpte.

ruleCards.title: Infinitive: -a
ruleCards.rule: The infinitive is the dictionary form. It usually ends in -a. Use it after a help verb and after att.
examples: We are going to live here.
ruleCards.watch: Group III verbs have no -a: bo, tro, må. And no att after a help verb: Jag vill äta, not Jag vill att äta.

fun.sv: Jag gillar att städa. Alltså, att titta på när andra städar.
fun.en: I like cleaning. I mean, watching other people clean.

ruleCards.title: Command form
ruleCards.rule: For Group II and IV verbs, drop the -a from the infinitive: stänga → Stäng! For Group I and III verbs, the command is the same as the infinitive: Lyssna! Bo!
ruleCards.watch: Add gärna to sound friendly: Ring mig gärna!

fun.sv: Sitt! Ligg! Stanna! Katten tittar på mig och går.
fun.en: Sit! Lie down! Stay! The cat looks at me and leaves.
fun.note: Sitta and ligga drop the -a (Sitt! Ligg!); stanna stays the same (Stanna!).

ruleCards.title: Help verbs + infinitive
ruleCards.rule: Kan, vill, ska, måste and brukar are help verbs. The verb after a help verb is always in the infinitive.
examples: She is going to travel to Sweden.
Jag brukar dricka te på morgonen.
I usually drink tea in the morning.
ruleCards.watch: Only the help verb is in the present: Jag vill äter is wrong. Brukar means “usually”.

fun.sv: Jag vill träna. Jag ska träna. Jag måste träna. Jag brukar sova.
fun.en: I want to exercise. I’m going to exercise. I must exercise. I usually sleep.

ruleCards.title: Borde, får, får inte
ruleCards.rule: Borde means “ought to, should”. Får means “may, is allowed to”. Får inte means “must not, is not allowed to”.

fun.sv: Du får ta en bulle. Du borde ta två. Du får inte ta alla.
fun.en: You may take one bun. You really ought to take two. You must not take all of them.

ruleCards.title: Behöver inte (never “måste inte”)
ruleCards.rule: To say something is not necessary, use behöver inte. Don’t say måste inte.
examples: We don’t need to book a table.
ruleCards.watch: English “must not” = får inte (or ska inte: Du ska inte röka här). English “don’t have to” = behöver inte.

fun.sv: Du behöver inte väcka mig. Katten gör det klockan fem.
fun.en: You don’t need to wake me up. The cat does it at five.

ruleCards.title: Kunde, ville, skulle
ruleCards.rule: The help verbs have past forms: kan → kunde, vill → ville, ska → skulle. The next verb is still in the infinitive.
examples: We were going to meet at three.
ruleCards.watch: Skulle vilja is the polite way to ask for something: Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe.

fun.sv: Jag skulle sova tidigt. Jag ville se ett avsnitt till. Jag kunde inte sluta.
fun.en: I was going to go to sleep early. I wanted to watch one more episode. I couldn’t stop.

ruleCards.title: Vet or känner?
ruleCards.rule: Both mean “know”. Vet is for facts and information. Känner is for people (and places you know well).
examples: Do you know where the station is?
ruleCards.watch: Känner mig / dig / sig means “feel”: Jag känner mig trött.

fun.sv: Jag känner min granne, men jag vet inte vad han heter.
fun.en: I know my neighbour, but I don’t know his name.
fun.note: Känner for the person, vet for the fact (his name).
